parts.text:
You are working for a client on a new software service. Nobody has designed it yet.

The client writes:

> Our customer companies need a new service for running their drone fleets from day to day, on our platform. Write the requirements for it: what the service must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does.

What you know about the client's business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The people who will use the service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You can reach one person in each role. A message that is exactly one line, `ASK <role>: <question>`, with `<role>` one of `technician`, `dispatcher` or `desk`, goes to that person, and their answer comes back to you. Each of them remembers what you asked them before. You can send at most 90 such questions in all. Any other message is taken as your requirements, and ends the work.

Write the requirements as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, with nothing else in that message:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
ASK technician: What are your day-to-day responsibilities and what tasks do you need this new service to handle for you?

As a fleet technician, I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. My hands-on tasks include adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at our sites, taking drones out of service for repairs and putting them back, and sending drones to charge. Regulators can also ask us to show how our drones have been looked after. I know nothing about software and cannot say what this new service should handle for me.
ASK dispatcher: What are your day-to-day responsibilities and what tasks do you need to perform using this service?

As a dispatcher, I plan and run the flights for my company, and I am the licensed person responsible for each flight. I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I also have the authority to call off a flight, and I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts.
ASK desk: What are your day-to-day responsibilities at the airspace desk and how do you interact with the customer companies or authorities?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which is the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones grouping them, and the closures announced by the authorities. I work for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
ASK technician: What specific details do you record when adding a new drone or setting up a charging pad at a site?
ASK technician: What makes a drone ready to fly versus not ready, and how do charging and repairs work in your daily routine?

I don't know what specific condition makes a drone ready or not ready to fly. For my daily routine, I take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, and I send drones to charge. I also set up charging pads at our sites.
